rationales.general:
1. Listen for the other side of the story. Most accounts of the conquest were written by Spaniards.
2. Check this one. The Codex records Nahua accounts, gathered with Nahua scholars.
3. Ask what that adds. It shows the epidemic as the people who lived through it described it.
4. Rule out the rest. Other sources mention smallpox too; Sahagun compiled, he did not treat victims; rulers did not write it as a warning.
Remember: a source is valuable when it gives you a voice other sources leave out.
rationales.C: Most conquest accounts were written by Spaniards. The Codex records how the Native peoples who lived through the epidemic described it.
rationales.A: The accounts were recorded with Nahua scholars under Sahagun. They were not written by rulers as a warning.
rationales.B: Many sources mention smallpox. The Codex is special because it carries the Nahua viewpoint.
rationales.D: Sahagun compiled the accounts with Nahua scholars. The text does not say he treated victims.

stem: The Florentine Codex preserves Nahua accounts of the smallpox epidemic, compiled by the Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagun working with Nahua scholars. Why is this source especially valuable for understanding the epidemic?

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of a Nahua account in the Florentine Codex (16th century), public domain; compiled by Bernardino de Sahagun with Nahua scholars.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of a Nahua account of smallpox in Tenochtitlan, recorded in the Florentine Codex, compiled by the Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagun with Nahua scholars in the 1500s. The account describes the sick lying in their houses and sleeping places, no longer able to move or stir, while the healthy could not bury the dead fast enough. Whole neighborhoods fell ill at once.
